schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    EMPID INT,
    NAME VARCHAR(255),
    SUPERVISOR INT,
    SALARY INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (EMPID),
    CHECK (EMPID <> SUPERVISOR),
    CHECK (SALARY >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE BONUS (
    EMPID INT,
    BONUS INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (EMPID),
    FOREIGN KEY (EMPID) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(EMPID),
    CHECK (BONUS >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2: SELECT E.NAME, B.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE E LEFT JOIN BONUS B ON E.EMPID = B.EMPID WHERE B.BONUS < 1000 OR B.EMPID IS NULL
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT E.NAME, B.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE E LEFT JOIN BONUS B ON E.EMPID = B.EMPID WHERE B.BONUS < 1000 OR B.EMPID IS NULL
counterexample: INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (EMPID, NAME, SUPERVISOR, SALARY) VALUES (1, 'John Doe', 2, 5000); INSERT INTO BONUS (EMPID, BONUS) VALUES (1, NULL);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because they join the EMPLOYEE and BONUS tables differently. Q1 checks for BONUS < 1000 or BONUS IS NULL, while Q2 checks for B.BONUS < 1000 or B.EMPID IS NULL. The difference arises when an employee has a NULL bonus in the BONUS table.
counterexample_dsp: Create an employee with a NULL bonus in the BONUS table. Q1 will include this employee in the result because of the BONUS IS NULL condition, while Q2 will exclude it because of the B.EMPID IS NULL condition.
